name: Baking soda and peroxide paste

lead: This paste mixes baking soda with hydrogen peroxide to brush teeth for a whiter look. The baking soda scrubs surface stain while the peroxide lightens the tooth.

Baking soda acts as a mild abrasive and acid buffer, and hydrogen peroxide oxidises coloured pigment molecules, so the pair is meant to give both stain removal and lightening. Commercial toothpastes have combined the two ingredients, and Wikipedia notes that peroxide can be mixed with baking soda and salt as a home-made toothpaste. Studies of the home-mixed paste itself were not identified.

paras: People mix a small amount into a paste and brush with it as an occasional substitute for or addition to regular toothpaste. Users generally describe results building over repeated uses. It is often paired with ordinary fluoride toothpaste on other days.

Hydrogen peroxide at higher concentrations can irritate or burn mucous membranes, and whitening commonly causes tooth sensitivity. Baking soda is described as low in abrasiveness, but concentration and brushing frequency are not controlled in home mixtures.

angle.text: Users brush with a baking soda and hydrogen peroxide paste to lift surface stain and lighten teeth. The baking soda scrubs gently while the peroxide bleaches pigment. Each ingredient has its own literature, while the home-mixed paste has little direct study.

lead: Baking soda and peroxide paste is a home-made tooth-cleaning mixture of sodium bicarbonate and hydrogen peroxide, used to lift surface stains from coffee, tea and tobacco so teeth look whiter and brighter. People choose it as a cheap alternative to whitening strips and whitening toothpaste. Wikipedia's toothpaste article notes that a baking soda and hydrogen peroxide paste was recommended for brushing as early as 1900 [1].

Each ingredient has its own role. Hydrogen peroxide is the most common active whitening agent in tooth whitening, working through free radicals that break down pigment molecules, while baking soda is described as a low-abrasive stain remover. Baking soda is one of several abrasives used in toothpaste to remove plaque and food, and Arm & Hammer sold a baking-soda tooth powder in the US until about 2000 [1][2]. The chain people describe is mild abrasion plus oxidation of pigment, leading to a whiter smile.

Studies of the home-mixed paste were not found. Regulators set limits on consumer peroxide: the EU limits retail hydrogen peroxide to 0.1 percent, and the US FDA endorses gels under 6 percent hydrogen peroxide.
infobox: Mild abrasion plus oxidation of pigment
Recommended for brushing as early as 1900 [1]

paras: Online communities describe the paste as a low-cost alternative to commercial whitening. Because mixing ratios, peroxide strength and frequency vary, the practice is not standardised and no preparation instructions are given here. A T Nation forum member describes brushing with baking soda or tooth powder and using 3 percent hydrogen peroxide as a mouthwash [3]; another forum post quotes a home dental formula that adds glycerin to baking soda [4].

Peroxide whitens through free radicals that break down pigment molecules, and a 2017 review cited on Wikipedia describes baking soda as an effective low-abrasive stain remover. Wikipedia says abrasion is the main way toothpaste removes stains and that whitening toothpaste cannot change natural tooth color or reverse discoloration beneath the surface [1]. Whether combining the two at home gives an additive effect has not been established.

Hydrogen peroxide at 10 percent or more can damage tissue and burn mucous membranes, and whitening commonly causes sensitivity. Household 3 percent peroxide is noted as potentially dangerous to the eye. Carbamide peroxide has been reported to increase enamel roughness and porosity. Toothpaste abrasiveness is rated by Relative Dentin Abrasivity, with products below 250 considered safe for lifelong use by the American Dental Association and ANSI, and overuse of abrasives may wear enamel [1]. Sodium bicarbonate's main listed hazard is serious eye irritation [2].

lore.intro: The mix appears in forum discussions of cheap, natural-sounding dental care.

claims.claim: Baking soda with peroxide keeps teeth clean and free of plaque without commercial toothpaste.

timeline.event: A baking soda and hydrogen peroxide paste is recommended for brushing. [1]
